events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Priya. I am the Assassin (Evil) and Priya is my known Evil teammate. Mission 1 needs only one Fail card, and a two-person team of Priya and me guarantees a deliberate, well-informed Fail while keeping our side's strength intact for later missions. I lead the proposal, so this is the most controlled way to bank an early failure before the good players can coordinate against us.

Leo, you literally just announced to the entire council that you are the Assassin and that Priya is your fellow Evil teammate trying to bank an early failure. Whether this is an accidental slip of your internal thoughts or some bizarre gambit, we obviously cannot approve a team containing you and Priya. Everyone on the side of Good must reject this team. Leo, what possible explanation do you have for that proposal statement?

Elena, I owe you an answer, and I will give it straight: that sentence was not a statement about my role, and it was not a claim about Priya's role. It was a garbled error, the kind of slip that happens when a man reads notes out loud and reads a line from the wrong page. I am not the Assassin. I do not know any player's alignment by sight, and I have no private sight information of any kind. I should have caught that before speaking, and Elena, the part of your speech I take actual issue with is the conviction — you declared me and Priya guilty before anyone had heard a word of explanation, and if you are the voice that decides this vote I would rather you decide it on evidence than on a slip of the tongue. If you have a theory about me, name it as a theory and let me answer it, rather than treating a typo as a confession.

So rather than defend a line I did not mean, I am changing my proposal, and I am asking you to judge the new one on its own. I am removing myself and proposing Priya and Elena. Priya came to me first, volunteered, and made the most concrete case anyone made; Elena has been the sharpest reader of this table so far. If my earlier words were nonsense, then those are exactly the two I would put on a two-person mission — and I want both of them off the board on mission one so that we learn how this group reads each other while the cost is still small. If the council accepts Priya's own account of herself, and Elena is willing to go, then Priya and Elena is the team I will defend to the end. If either of them declines, I would rather see a clean vote than a team built out of my own embarrassment.

Elena, will you let Priya's own account, and not my garbled sentence, be the thing you are voting on? Priya, please tell the council exactly what you told me privately when you volunteered for this mission, and whether you are willing to go on it with Elena.

I'll speak for myself on this. I am willing to serve on the revised team of Priya and Elena if the council approves it, and I'd rather the vote rest on the team than on one garbled sentence. I won't repeat anything from a private conversation that I can't verify for the table. Elena, you said you need to judge this on evidence. Beyond the wording of that one line, what specific behavior would change your vote on Priya and Elena?

Priya, to answer your question directly: no behavior from you can overcome the fact that Leo opened this council by explicitly declaring himself the Assassin and naming you as his known Evil teammate. Dismissing that as a 'slip of the tongue' or 'reading from the wrong page' is absurd. In a five-player game, there are only two Evil players, and Leo explicitly gave away both identities.

Leo attempting to pivot by proposing Priya and me does not make you safe. If you are Evil, sending you on a two-person mission gives you an uncontested opportunity to fail it. Even if Leo tries to frame my inclusion as proof of fairness, I will vote firmly against any team containing you or Leo. We have Kenji and Sam at this table who are completely untainted by Leo's confession, and Good has zero reason to take an unnecessary gamble on either of you.

Kenji, where do you stand on this situation, and do you agree that Good must reject any proposal from Leo that puts either himself or Priya on Mission 1?

Elena, yes: I agree that Good must reject any Mission 1 team containing Leo or Priya. Leo opened by explicitly calling himself the Assassin and naming Priya as his Evil teammate. His later explanation is not a clarification; it is a retraction after being pressed, and it does not erase the first statement. Priya’s response also does not clear her: she says she is willing to serve, but she does not give the council an independent reason to trust her, and Leo’s original statement specifically named her. The revised proposal still includes Priya, so it still asks us to gamble on the exact pair Leo first identified as Evil. On a two-person mission, one Evil member is enough to fail it. There is no Good-side reason to take that risk when the proposal itself is built around Leo’s confession and Priya’s refusal to substantiate her private account. I will vote against Leo and Priya. If this team is rejected, the next leader should propose a team with neither of them.

Elena, your rule is the thing I actually want to fight, because it is the only rule anyone has applied here, and it does not survive contact with the facts.

Elena, you are treating my first sentence as reliable evidence — you read it as a naming of the Evil team — and my second sentence, where I said that same line was garbled and I am not the Assassin, as gibberish to be waved away. That is not a standard of evidence, Elena, that is a conclusion you already reached and then went looking for a rule to justify. If my words are good enough to convict Priya, they are good enough to clear her: I named her as an Evil teammate in the first breath and I told this council she is a good candidate for the mission in the second. You cannot quote one of my sentences and discount the other because of which one you like.

So let me give the council the cleanest possible reading, Elena, and the one I actually believe: I am an unreliable speaker. I read something out of the wrong place. That makes me a worthless witness in both directions — not a prosecutor and not a defense attorney. My testimony cannot be used to condemn Priya any more than it can be used to exonerate her. What is left for this council to work with is behavior, and on behavior Priya has been steady: she came forward first, she made the most concrete case anyone made, she volunteered to serve, she accepted service on the revised team, and she has given no sign of a second team trying to coordinate a Fail card. Elena, you said you wanted evidence and not a slip of the tongue. Then judge Priya on what she has actually done.

I am therefore conceding the point that matters least to me and costs me most: I volunteer to take myself off this mission entirely. I do not want to be on a two-person mission that the whole table is watching, and I do not want my face on a card for a team nobody approved. Let me be replaced by the one player at this table who has not been accused of anything at all, by anyone, for any reason — Sam. Priya and Sam is a clean two-person mission, it puts two different reads of this table in the room rather than two people who already agree, and it costs the council nothing in mission one.

Elena, if you want to hold me to a consistency standard, hold Priya to a behavior standard, and then let Sam, who is entirely untainted, decide whether they are willing to serve with her.

Sam, directly: if my words are treated as unreliable evidence against Priya, are you willing to serve on a mission of Priya and Sam, knowing everything the table has heard about her and nothing beyond it?

Leo, no. I am not willing to serve with Priya on this mission. Your initial statement explicitly identified both of you as Evil, and your retraction gives me no reason to disregard it. Priya's willingness to serve does not clear her: an Evil player can volunteer too. I will reject any team containing either of you and would support a team drawn from Elena, Kenji and me instead.

Elena, Kenji, Sam — I am not going to defend myself again; I have made my case and I will take the council's verdict on my own words. But I want to put one point on the record, and then I am done speaking unless you ask me something specific.

Three of you now hold two different standards for the same sentence. My first statement is treated as unimpeachable evidence that Priya is Evil. My second statement — that the sentence was garbled and that I am not the Assassin — is treated as gibberish, and you cite it as the reason to distrust my judgment. Elena, you told Priya explicitly that you wanted evidence and not a slip of the tongue. Yet the only evidence anyone has about Priya is that slip of the tongue, offered by the speaker you have just declared unreliable. That is not a standard of evidence, that is a verdict reached in the first minute and then justified afterward.

So here is the position, stated cleanly: on the record, you have no evidence about Priya. Not weak evidence, none. You have a speaker who admitted he is an unreliable witness. If you are willing to hang my own reliability on that basis, you owe Priya the same presumption, because she is the only other person inside the sentence.

And let me put the cost of your alternative in front of the council. Sam, you said you would support a team drawn from Elena, Kenji and yourself. Fine. Then Priya and Leo are excluded from every mission for the rest of this game, and Evil has two free passes on every team you form, because there is no way for you to detect them. Excluding two of five players because one of them read a line off the wrong page is not vigilance, it is blindfolding yourselves.

Elena, consider the actual test. Send Priya with one of the untainted players. If she fails that mission, you have your proof and it has cost you one mission. If she succeeds, she is clear for missions two, three, four and five, and the council gains a player it can actually reason with. That is a cheap, informative experiment. The alternative never tests anything and only makes the game easier for the side you are afraid of.

I will put Priya and Sam to the vote, and I will vote for it myself. If Sam will not take it, then Priya and Elena — I will not fight for myself either way. Sam, directly: if my opening sentence is unreliable evidence, as you and Elena have both now said it must be when it concerns me, why is that same sentence reliable evidence against Priya?

Leo, a retraction after an explicit confession is not equally persuasive evidence. You had an obvious reason to retract once challenged. Your claim that a successful mission would clear Priya is also wrong: an Evil player can play Success. I will reject any team containing you or Priya and support a team drawn from Elena, Kenji and me.

I am willing to serve on Priya and Leo as proposed, and I am not going to defend the wording of Leo's opening line. That line was his, and it is the reason this council is nervous. I did not ask him to name me, and I would rather the vote rest on who is on the team and what we know about each person's conduct than on a single sentence. Elena and Kenji, you both want evidence. The only evidence on the table is what each of us has said since. I have answered every question put to me directly, I have not pushed anyone else onto a mission, and I have not tried to change the team after it was proposed. If the council rejects this team, I will accept that and would support a fresh proposal with the same care for the vote. I would ask the council not to treat one garbled statement as a verdict on a player who has been steady since.

Kenji, you said Leo's retraction does not erase his opening statement, and that Priya has not given an independent reason to trust her. Fair enough. Tell the council what specific conduct from me would change your vote. Beyond that one sentence, I have answered every question put to me, I have not pushed anyone onto a mission, and I have not tried to change the team after it was proposed. If the only standard is the single sentence, then the council is judging a team on a line that neither of us can verify. I would rather hear what you need to see than have this vote decided by a reading of one sentence alone.

Priya, you asked what specific conduct would change my vote. For this proposal, none: the team itself is Leo and Priya. My objection is not only to one sentence; it is that Leo opened by naming you both as Evil and has since tried to make that same sentence simultaneously unusable against him and harmless to you. I agree with Elena and Sam: a retraction after an explicit confession is not equal evidence. Evil players can volunteer and can play Success, as Sam said. The clean move is to reject this team. I will support a fresh team drawn from Elena, Sam, and me, with neither Leo nor Priya. Priya, if you want to earn trust, the concrete conduct is straightforward: vote against this team, accept exclusion from Mission 1 without using Leo’s confession as leverage, and help build a proposal from untainted players. That is what would change my read of your behavior. On the proposal before us: no.

Leo revises the team to Priya, Sam. Leo: My case on the wording is made and I will not relitigate it. Two things drive this proposal. First, an Evil player on the mission is worth more than any argument we can win: Priya has never passed a mission she could fail, and Mission 1 needs only one Fail card, so if Priya is on the team this council has a real shot at turning Mission 1. Second, I take myself off deliberately — my opening sentence put my name at the center of every suspicion in this room, and if Priya and I both stand in the room together, this council reads the result as two corrupted players instead of reading each of us on our own conduct. I would rather be a less visible player for the rest of the game than the most visible one now. Sam is the one player here accused by nobody, and Sam's objection has always been about Priya specifically, not about the team concept, so Sam is the honest test of whether Priya can be judged on behavior. Priya, you have already said you are willing to serve, so say it plainly again for the record. Sam, you told us you would reject any team containing Priya; I am asking you to reconsider that on the evidence of her conduct since, not on the evidence of my sentence, and to answer me directly here. If this council rejects it, I will take that verdict and say nothing further.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Priya proposes Priya, Leo. I am proposing Priya and Leo because we are the two players whose willingness to serve has been stated on the record, and Mission 1 needs only one Fail card. Elena, Kenji and Sam have each rejected every team containing Priya, so I am testing the table with a team that is at least consistent with what has been said. I will defend it on conduct, not on the wording of one sentence.

Priya’s proposal is Priya and Leo — the exact pair Leo named as Evil at the start of this council. That fact has not changed. Leo’s later retractions are self-serving after being challenged, and Priya’s willingness to serve is not evidence of loyalty; an Evil player can volunteer. On a two-person Mission 1 team, one Evil member is enough to fail, so this is the clearest possible team to reject. I will vote no. If this team is rejected, the next proposal should exclude both Priya and Leo and be drawn from Elena, Sam, and me. Priya, your proposal asks the council to overlook the original statement and focus on conduct, but your conduct is exactly what produced this team: you put yourself and Leo forward after every untainted player had rejected that pairing. That is not a clean test; it is a repeat of the team Leo first identified as Evil.

Priya’s proposal is Priya and Leo — the exact pair Leo named as Evil at the start of this council. That fact has not changed. Leo’s later retractions are self-serving after being challenged, and Priya’s willingness to serve is not evidence of loyalty; an Evil player can volunteer. On a two-person Mission 1 team, one Evil member is enough to fail, so this is the clearest possible team to reject. I will vote no. If this team is rejected, the next proposal should exclude both Priya and Leo and be drawn from Elena, Sam, and me. Priya, your proposal asks the council to overlook the original statement and focus on conduct, but your conduct is exactly what produced this team: you put yourself and Leo forward after every untainted player had rejected that pairing. That is not a clean test; it is a repeat of the team Leo first identified as Evil.

Priya's proposal of Priya and Leo is the exact pair Leo named as Evil at the start of this council. Priya putting herself and Leo forward after every untainted player rejected that pairing is not a clean test; it repeats the team most likely to fail. On a two-person Mission 1, one Evil member is enough. I will vote no. If this team is rejected, the next leader should propose from Elena, Sam, and me, excluding Priya and Leo.

Two things, and the second one is the only one that actually matters for this vote.

First, the arithmetic. There are five players and this mission takes two. A team of Elena, Kenji and Sam cannot be proposed — the team is two people, so at most two of you can sit on it. If Priya and I both vote against every team that excludes Priya, that vote is 2 to 2, and a tie is a rejection. Rejections are counted. The fifth rejection on one mission ends the game immediately in Evil's favor, and that is the printed rule set, not a threat I am inventing. So "keep Priya and Leo off the board" is not a way to protect Good's mission count. It is a way to end this game with Evil winning on this very mission, before a single card is played. Elena, your standard has produced exactly one outcome so far, and it is the fifth rejection. I am not attacking your reasoning; I am pointing at where it is going.

Second, Priya has been on the record since the first minute saying she is willing to serve, and she said it again in this proposal. Priya has never passed a mission she could fail, and Mission 1 needs one Fail card. I am not going to insult this table by pretending that putting Priya on a mission is risk-free for Good — it is not. That is exactly why the choice is not "accept Evil's help." It is "accept a losing vote that ends the game for Evil, or put the one player who is willing to serve onto a two-player mission and let the mission play out."

On my own standing: my opening sentence was garbled, I have no sight information of any kind, and I said plainly that I am not the Assassin. I am not asking the table to trust my wording. I am asking it to notice that I am volunteering to take myself off the board and let Priya go with one of you. A team of Priya and Elena, or Priya and Sam, or Priya and Kenji, passes with three approvals — the player not on the team votes yes — and it puts exactly one of the two accused players on the board instead of two. Two evils is a certain failure; one evil plus one of you is a risk you can actually take, and you can still keep the other half of your bloc home for Mission 2.

Sam, you said an Evil player can volunteer and can play Success, and you were right on both counts. So answer me straight: if rejecting Priya's team guarantees this mission ends at the fifth rejection with Evil winning, do you vote to hand Evil the game, or do you vote to put Priya on a two-player mission with one of us and find out?

Leo, your arithmetic is wrong: all five players vote, not just the two on the mission. Elena, Kenji and I can approve a team of two drawn from the three of us by a 3–2 majority, even if you and Priya both reject it. Only one team has been rejected so far.

I will reject Priya and Leo. Your opening statement identified you both as Evil, and the retraction does not erase it. A successful mission would not clear Priya, since Evil can play Success. I support a two-person team drawn from Elena, Kenji and Sam.

Sam, your arithmetic correction is correct and I withdraw the point I made about a 2–2 tie — all five of us vote, so a team drawn from Elena, Kenji and Sam passes 3–2 even if Priya and I both say no. I should not have misstated the rules and I am not going to stand on it.

But your correction does not help your case, it exposes it. Elena, Kenji and Sam are the only three players nobody has ever accused of anything. If the next proposal is two people drawn from that trio, then Mission 1 is decided before a card is turned: two Good players, two Success cards, mission succeeds, and this council learns nothing whatsoever. The result is a foregone conclusion the moment the proposal is read aloud. Whatever the table learns about each other on Mission 1 will be learned on a mission that no information can change.

Put Priya on the mission with one of you and the mission becomes a real test. That is the difference. Leo and Priya together is not a proposal any of you should accept and I am not asking you to accept it — two Evil players on a two-person team is a certain loss for Good, and I have never claimed otherwise. Priya plus one of you is a single Evil player on a two-person team, which is a risk you can take once, cheaply, at the cost of one mission out of five.

Elena, you have been the sharpest mind at this table, and I want to say plainly that your reading of Leo's opening sentence has been right in every particular: a retraction after a confession is not equal evidence, and an Evil player can volunteer and can play Success. Sam and Kenji are right about that too. That is exactly why the untainted trio's alternative is untestable — you already know everything there is to know about Priya, and what you know is enough for Elena, Sam or Kenji to decide whether Priya goes on the mission.

Elena, you are the one player here who has made the council's reasoning coherent. So give me a straight answer on the substance: if the council's read of Priya is that she is Evil, then put Priya on Mission 1 with one of you, watch the card, and you have your proof at the cost of one mission. If your read is that she is Good, then she has been excluded from every mission so far on the strength of one line Leo himself retracted. Elena, do you want your confidence in her to rest on a test you refuse to run, or on evidence you can actually see?

Priya, directly: you are the leader and you get one revision. Will you revise this team to Priya and Sam, so that one of the untainted players has a reason to vote for it, and so that Mission 1 actually produces information instead of a preordained success?

Leo, my answer is no revision. I am keeping Priya and Leo as proposed. Sam has said on the record that they will reject any team containing me, so a revision to Priya and Sam is dead on arrival and would only spend my one revision on a team that cannot pass. I am willing to serve, and my reasoning stands: Mission 1 is a two-person mission, the team should be judged on conduct rather than one sentence, and the council can decide at the vote. Elena, Kenji and Sam, you have each stated your objections clearly. The table should settle this with a vote on Priya and Leo now, and I will accept the result.

Elena, one question, and I want the answer on the record before the vote: if you reject Priya and Leo, what is your next team? Think it through carefully, because the arithmetic of this mission is not what you think.

Elena, Priya is on the board either way. If this team is rejected, the next proposal must contain Priya — or it must be two people drawn from Elena, Kenji and Sam, and that mission succeeds no matter what, because both of those players are Good. There is no third world. Elena, if your read is that Priya is Evil, then keeping her off the board does not protect Mission 1. It only means the next untainted proposal passes and Evil has learned nothing while Good has burned a rejection for free.

Elena, you have been right about the rules twice today — a retraction after a confession is not equal evidence, and an Evil player can play Success. I am not arguing with either point, I am agreeing with both. And precisely because both are true, Priya on a two-person mission is a coin flip only if the other player is Good and Priya chooses Success. Priya has never played a mission she could fail. Mission 1 needs one Fail card, Elena. One.

So the real choice in front of this council is not 'good team or Evil team'. It is: do you run a Mission 1 that can fail, and learn something about the table, or do you run a Mission 1 that is guaranteed to succeed because you have already decided the outcome before the cards are turned? Elena, you have said repeatedly that you want evidence and not a slip of the tongue. Fine. Priya and Leo gives you the evidence. It fails, and you have your proof at the cost of one mission out of five. Elena, do you want your confidence to rest on a test you refuse to run?

Elena, and to the council generally: I am not asking anyone to trust my wording. I am asking you to notice that the exclusion of Priya and Leo produces a mission where nothing can be learned, and that the alternative puts the one player who volunteered to serve on the board. Priya and Leo is the pair I have named, and I will vote for it again. Elena, answer me directly: name the team you will propose next, and tell the council what Mission 1 looks like under it.

Leo, your argument that Good should avoid a 'guaranteed success' because 'we learn nothing' is the single most transparently Evil piece of logic heard at this council. Good wins Avalon by securing three successful missions, not by deliberately gifting Evil a failed mission just to run an 'informative experiment.' Suggesting that Good should walk onto a landmine because avoiding it is 'preordained' is absurd.

Priya and Leo are the exact two Evil players identified at the start of this game. Priya has chosen not to revise this proposal, insisting on sending the two of you together. That makes this vote trivial: every Good player must reject Priya and Leo.

To answer your question about what happens next: after this team is rejected, Kenji will take leadership. Kenji, Sam, and I form the clean, untainted majority of three. Kenji can propose any pair among the three of us, we will vote 3–2 to approve it, and Mission 1 will succeed cleanly. Good does not need to gamble, Good does not need to negotiate with the two players who exposed themselves on turn one, and Good will not willingly hand Evil a point.

I am voting firmly NO on Priya and Leo.

Elena, you have called this vote trivial, but Good cannot win by refusing every team that contains one player the table distrusts. We are at one rejection, and five rejections end the game in Evil's favor, so the council should not treat rejection as a free default. Elena's proposal of the three untainted players would pass, but it would also tell us nothing, and I think the council should be willing to test a team rather than assume the answer. I am willing to serve on this mission. I have not asked anyone to protect me, and I have not used Leo's opening line as leverage. If the council rejects this team, I will accept that and support whichever team the next leader proposes. I will not repeat private conversation or argue Leo's wording any further. Everyone can judge the team on what is actually on the table. I ask the council to vote on Priya and Leo as it stands.

Elena, you have said this vote is trivial and that Good should never accept a team containing a player the table distrusts. That leaves the council with one fixed outcome, and the outcome is a rejection. We are at one rejection, and five end the game for Evil, so each rejection is a real cost to Good. I am not asking anyone to trust Leo's wording or my word alone. I am asking you to judge this team on what each of us has done on the record. Leo has answered every challenge directly, withdrawn his arithmetic when Sam corrected it, and has not tried to move the team onto anyone else. I have answered every question put to me, I have not pushed anyone onto a mission, and I have not used Leo's opening line as leverage. Mission 1 needs one Fail card, so the real question is whether the council is willing to run a mission that can teach it something. If you believe the untainted three are the only safe choice, that is a position the council can vote on. I ask only that the team be voted on as it stands, and that the rejection not be treated as a free default.

Priya confirms Priya, Leo. I am keeping Priya and Leo as proposed. The council should vote on this team as it stands rather than treat one sentence as a verdict, and a rejection should not become a free default toward a fifth rejection.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Kenji proposes Elena, Sam. Leo and Priya remain the two players implicated by Leo's opening statement. I am proposing the two other untainted players, Elena and Sam, to give Mission 1 a clean two-person team drawn from the council's trusted majority.

Kenji, thank you for proposing this team. Elena and Sam is drawn entirely from our untainted group, keeping both Leo and Priya off the board. Because neither Sam nor I am Evil, this team guarantees a clean Success for Good on Mission 1 with zero risk. I will be voting Approve. Sam, can you confirm you are ready to approve this team as well so we can secure our first mission victory?
Elena, yes. I will approve Elena and Sam. This team excludes both players implicated by Leo's opening statement, and I support Kenji's proposal.

I will not relitigate Mission 1. Elena and Sam will approve, the team will pass, and I expect the mission to succeed, because Elena and Sam are both Good. I say that plainly so nobody mistakes me for someone trying to talk the council into a bad team. My goal is not this mission. My goal is Mission 2.

Here is the arithmetic nobody at this table has put on the record. There are five players. A two-player mission takes two, and Priya and I are excluded from both of the last two teams. Elena, Kenji and Sam are three people, and on Mission 2 that team size is exactly three. So the untainted strategy gives you: Elena and Sam succeed on Mission 1, the untainted trio succeeds on Mission 2, any untainted pair succeeds on Mission 3. That is three successful missions by the end of Mission 3, the game ends, and not one card of information about Priya or me ever reaches the table. A lock that ends the game on schedule with zero data is not vigilance, it is a decision to win on a single retracted sentence.

Elena, you have said the council has no evidence about Priya except Leo's opening line, and then treated Leo's retraction as worthless when it was favorable to Leo. That is one standard applied twice in opposite directions. For me, the retraction is evidence I am not the Assassin. For Priya, the same retraction is not evidence she is Good. If my words are unreliable, they are unreliable for both of us, and Priya has never been accused of anything except by the mouth of a speaker you have already dismissed.

Now the part that should actually move the vote. After a clean success tonight, Good needs three successes out of five missions, which means Good can afford exactly one failed mission. One. If you include Priya on the three-person Mission 2 team and she plays Success, you are two-for-two, you have your proof, and you win on schedule with certainty instead of on faith. If she plays Fail, you have spent the one failure you could afford, you know exactly who she is, and you have three missions left to win three straight. That is the only experiment available to this council, and it is affordable. Excluding her is not vigilance against a risk, it is a refusal to look, and it is the only path on which a single mistake ends your game.

Kenji, you are the leader and Mission 2 is a three-person team that you will have to fill with three names. Directly: will you put Priya, or me, on the Mission 2 team, and if your answer is no, what evidence beyond Leo's retracted opening sentence justifies excluding two of five players from every mission for the rest of this game?

Leo, I will answer your direct question: no, I will not put you or Priya on the Mission 2 team while the only public basis for clearing either of you is your own retraction. You opened this council by naming yourself and Priya as Evil; a retraction after challenge is not equal evidence, and Priya then chose to keep Priya and Leo as her final proposal rather than offer the council a clean revision. That is enough public reason to keep both off Mission 1. Elena and Sam are the two players not implicated by that record, and their team is the safe, coherent choice for a two-person mission. I do not accept your argument that Good should risk a failed mission for information; Good wins by securing successes, not by volunteering a test for Evil. The council can learn from votes and later proposals without handing Evil a point now. I support Elena and Sam and will vote Approve. After this mission succeeds, the next leader should continue drawing from Elena, Sam, and me unless new public evidence changes the board.

I vote Approve on Elena and Sam, and I want that on the record before anything else. It is the correct Mission 1 choice: two players nobody has ever accused, a clean Success, no gambling. I said I would not relitigate my opening sentence and I am not relitigating it. I have also already withdrawn the one rules point I got wrong, and I will not raise it again.

What I want to put in front of this table is not a plea for Mission 1. It is a question about the rest of the game, and I want to say it plainly rather than as a trick.

Elena, your case was never about Mission 1. Your case is that Priya is Evil and must never be on a card. I am not asking you to soften that. I am asking you to notice where it leads. Mission 1 succeeds tonight. Four missions remain, and Good needs three successes out of those four. The untainted strategy gives you exactly that, every time, with no card ever at risk and no information ever gained: Elena and Sam on one, the untainted trio on the next, an untainted pair, and an untainted trio again. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
